rv.q: If you don’t understand why Coward is hailed as a genius – and Scott as the man of the moment - here’s your proof.
The party’s over, and Scott’s extravagant loneliness is unforgettable.
Andrew Scott is glorious in this revival of Noël Coward's chaotic Thirties caper.
The bisexual update adds some zest and surprise to a play that can feel just a bit dated when played straight.
There is more, though, to this triumph than great Scott.
It's a brilliant, subtle reading at the heart of a revelatory staging that finds the pathos beneath the patter in this bittersweet play.
Andrew Scott gives a virtuosic performance in Noël Coward’s imperishable 1943 comedy.
The performances are superb across the board, and I have never seen the careering farce-momentum that the piece develops played with a lovelier disciplined abandon.
After a lively start, things stall with the gay love scene.
His panache fills the entire theatre.
Scott locates the substance within Coward's theatrical soufflé and manages something quite astonishing: amidst the fusillade of laughs, he opens a window on to this play's fretful heart.
It lifts a deceptively light and ludicrous comedy that, 80 years on, has retained its fizz, into something delicately profound.
It is a wonderfully enjoyable few hours in the theatre, which, as it should, brings comedy, but also tragedy, too.
The director Matthew Warchus’s richly entertaining take on the play has, in the role of Garry, a singular actor in the fast-rising TV name Andrew Scott.
His attempt to turn it into a crowd-pleasing pantomime full of high farce and big laughs must be counted a success.
Aside from being touching, beautifully staged, fantastically performed and well-observed, Present Laughter is just so, so funny.
Matthew Warchus has done it with this cracking production of Noël Coward’s 1939 comedy Present Laughter.

cn.t: Andrew Scott delivers a virtuosic, career-defining performance in Matthew Warchus's glorious revival of Coward's comedy. Critics hail the production's hilarity and a revelatory gender-switch that makes the play feel fresh and relevant.
